title: Every spiritual blessing (Ephesians 1:3–14)
hook: a long sentence of praise: chosen, adopted, redeemed, sealed
carry: to the praise of his glory
tomorrow: Paul prays for friends. what does he ask for, if not a fix?

segments.voice: Galatians closed on a farmer's patience: in due season we shall reap. A new letter opens today, Ephesians, and its first word is a blessing.
screen: `IN DUE SEASON WE SHALL REAP.` → `A NEW LETTER: EPHESIANS.`

segments.voice: A blessing over a cup of coffee sounds like a lot, until you know the habit behind it. In Jewish tradition there are blessings for bread, for wine, for fruit, even for thunder, and one for ordinary things like a drink: by whose word all things came to be. Each begins, in English, Blessed are you, Lord our God. Now open Ephesians. Its first words: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ." Some readers hear the same shape.
screen: `A BLESSING OVER COFFEE?` → `BREAD, WINE, FRUIT, THUNDER.` → `BLESSED BE THE GOD AND FATHER.`

segments.voice: Today's question: what do you do with a good thing? Paul's answer is to say so, to God, and he can't stop. Some readers take verses three to fourteen as one long Greek sentence, gift piled on gift. Chosen: "he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world." Adopted, the word from three days ago. Redeemed: "In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins." Sealed with the Holy Spirit, a deposit on what's still to come. And under it all, a refrain like a chorus: "to the praise of his glory." The neighbor next door has the same instinct, in its own words. In the Talmud, Rabbi Meir teaches that a person should say a hundred blessings every day. That's the thing to tell a friend tonight. A hundred means noticing bread, water, waking up, the first fruit of a season, a storm rolling in. Shared ground, and it's wide: Jews and Christians both answer good things by blessing God for them. Here's the honest difference. Paul's blessing runs through Jesus; every gift in his list comes "in Christ." Jewish blessings bless God as King of the universe, and Judaism does not share the Christian faith in Jesus as the Messiah. One habit of thanks, two traditions, and a real difference neither needs to hide.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU DO WITH A GOOD THING?` · `CHOSEN, ADOPTED, REDEEMED, SEALED.` · `A HUNDRED BLESSINGS A DAY.` · `THE DIFFERENCE: IN CHRIST.` · then, large: `TO THE PRAISE OF HIS GLORY.`

segments.voice: Count your blessings slowly, on your fingers: something you ate today, someone who spoke to you, something you saw. Give each one a full breath before you move to the next. If you pray, you can close each with Paul's refrain: to the praise of his glory.
Every spiritual blessing. The opening of Ephesians: chosen, adopted, redeemed, sealed, poured out in one long rush of praise.
Hold onto this: to the praise of his glory, the chorus under every gift. Be well.

v3 wisdom / unity thread: neighbor tradition is Judaism, in its own sources, paraphrased (no public-domain translation quoted): Menachot 43b (Rabbi Meir, a person is obliged to say a hundred blessings every day); Mishnah Berakhot 6:1–3 (blessings over fruit, wine, bread; shehakol, 'by whose word all things came to be', for other foods and drinks) and 9:2 (over thunder). The opening formula is given in English without quotation marks ('Blessed are you, Lord our God'; the full formula adds 'King of the universe', which the teach names). Shared ground: answering gifts by blessing God. Honest difference: Paul blesses 'in Christ'; Judaism does not share the Christian faith in Jesus as Messiah. Confirm with a Christian Keeper and, ideally, a Jewish reader that both are fairly stated and nothing ranks either.
The claim that Ephesians 1:3 has the shape of a Jewish berakhah is hedged ('some readers hear the same shape'); confirm.
'Some readers take verses three to fourteen as one long Greek sentence' is hedged; confirm.

Election: the lesson quotes 'chosen' without unpacking it; churches read predestination and election in different ways (Reformed, Arminian, Catholic, Orthodox). A Keeper may want a short line if this is felt to be missing.
Gloss 'Ephesians … traditionally in Ephesus': some early manuscripts lack 'at Ephesus' in 1:1; hedged with 'traditionally'.
